structure.title: First essay · Who first had the right to name a virtue?
structure.text: Nietzsche proposes two accounts of moral naming. In one, powerful people call their own traits good. In another, people unable to strike back develop a vocabulary in which the powerful can finally be condemned.

structure.title: Second essay · How could an animal learn to promise?
structure.text: Debt, punishment and memory supply a harsh prehistory for responsibility. Nietzsche asks what happens when aggressive energies once discharged outwardly have to find an object inside the person who feels them.

structure.title: Third essay · Why would anyone want to renounce pleasure?
structure.text: Artists, philosophers, priests and scholars put the ascetic ideal to different uses. The investigation turns on a disturbing possibility. A painful explanation for suffering can command loyalty simply because it gives suffering a meaning.

people.name: Ressentiment
people.role: An injury kept alive in judgment
people.text: Nietzsche imagines a blocked desire for retaliation gaining creative power. It invents a moral scale on which the person who inflicted the injury can appear contemptible even while retaining every worldly advantage.

people.name: The creditor and debtor
people.text: What begins as an obligation that can be paid or exacted becomes a model for guilt. Nietzsche uses the kinship of words for debt and guilt to ask what survived when their social setting changed.

people.name: The ascetic priest
people.role: A sufferer who offers suffering a meaning
people.text: In the third essay the priest can tell a tormented person where to look for the cause of his pain. Receiving an explanation can itself be a relief. Nietzsche asks what else that explanation does to someone who leaves believing he has found the culprit in himself.

context.title: Genealogies argue about value
context.text: An origin story can loosen a value's claim to be self-evident. Nietzsche still has to show what the value does now. His dramatic reconstructions are proposed interpretations whose historical evidence and philosophical force can be assessed separately.

notice.text: Separate the origin of a practice from its later use.
notice.why: Punishment acquires many purposes in different hands. Explaining the present justification for a penalty therefore tells us surprisingly little about why that penalty first appeared.

notice.text: Ask what relief a diagnosis offers its patient.
notice.why: The ascetic priest gives pain an address and an explanation. Even an accusation against oneself can bring relief when the alternative is having no idea at all why one suffers.

opening: A person who cannot strike back can still declare the enemy evil and make helplessness sound virtuous. Nietzsche asks how much of our moral language may have developed through transformations like that. He digs beneath guilt, punishment, and self-denial, looking for the desires that respectable explanations conceal. His history is deliberately provocative, and its claims need resisting as well as following. The disturbance comes from seeing qualities we praise acquire an ancestry that their admirers would rather leave out of the family story.
